title: Кофе со снотворным  (Coffee with Sleeping Drops)

segments.t: Back at Claude Monet, Louis delivers a cup of coffee spiked with sleeping drops to German's office, and Senya and Fedya sneak in as soon as the boss slumps over his desk.
Лезь давай к нему в карман.
Да я руку не могу достать.
Let's walk through each line of the office infiltration.

'German Mikhailovich, here is your coffee.' Louis frames that thought plainly here: notice how Russian needs no word for "am", "is", or "are" in the present — placing the words side by side says it all.
'Just the way you like it.' Louis counters wryly beside Senya, watching Senya's face to see how the news lands.
'Why are you standing there, go on.' Senya points to this direct detail in reply: "stoish" means "stand" (from "stoyat"), giving the line its exact edge.

'And why does it have to be me right away?' Fedya shapes the reaction before Senya: putting the question word "pochemu" right at the front of the line lets Senya hear the point of the question on the very first beat.
'Let's play rock, paper, scissors for it.' Fedya pushes back briskly without any doubt, steering the talk right where he wants it.
'We already flipped a coin.' Senya highlights one vivid term in earnest: "monetku" means "coin" (from "monetka"), giving the line its exact edge.

'Maybe we should play the cities game too?' Fedya shares that remark at once: Russian keeps the exact word order of a normal statement here, turning it into a question for Louis purely through rising pitch at the end.
Лезь давай к нему в карман.
'Go on, reach into his pocket.' Senya steps in pointedly without any doubt, grounding the moment in plain reality.
'It is very funny to you, is it?' Fedya favors this clear detail with Louis: "smeshno" means "ridiculous", and it carries the main weight of what Fedya is saying.
'You had better help me instead.' Fedya delivers the reply plainly here: spoken Russian trims this down to just 4 words, dropping the extra helper words that English has to spell out.
'Well, what are you doing in here?' Louis questions bluntly what Fedya is actually getting at here.
Да я руку не могу достать.
'I cannot get my hand back out.' Fedya frames one memorable expression right here: "ruku" means "hand" (from "ruka"), giving the line its exact edge.

'I am afraid that he will wake up right now.' Fedya phrases the reaction plainly here: the "-sya" ending on "prosnyotsya" ("right") turns the action inward or makes it happen between people naturally.
'He will not wake up, he is sleeping soundly.' Senya counters boldly around Louis, grounding the moment in plain reality. Now let's hear the whole scene again from start to finish.
Лезь давай к нему в карман.
Да я руку не могу достать.
Notice how Russian orders the hand game as 'rock, scissors, paper', and uses the indirect form when saying 'it is funny to you'. Until next time!
